title: NeuroFlux p95 burst & fallback discovery
summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets for short vs long streaming responses, concurrent stream sizing, burst capacity and graceful degradation. NeuroFlux described current on-prem infra constraints, regulatory desire for VPC/private option, and an in-house microservice that emits 12-15k tokens/min per model during peak experiments. Redwood AE/SE outlined hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, autoscaling/burst pools, prefix/KV cache benefits, and suggested a phased pilot (hosted eval -> dedicated pilot -> private/Governed deploy). Next steps include sample benchmark plan, security docs, and pricing sketch.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-12-09
Start: 16:30 PST
Duration: 48m (approx)
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lina Zhou (Redwood SE), Tom Nguyen (Redwood CSM), Aisha Rahman (NeuroFlux, Head of ML), Diego Morales (Platform Eng), Priya Kapoor (SRE), Ben Chu (CTO joined 00:18:10)

Summary (auto): short vs streaming p95 targets, concurrent streams estimate, test harness and benchmark spreadsheet link requested. Action items at end.

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick roll call?
[00:00:05] Aisha: hi, hey, aisha here. we moved us to mountain time so apologies if i'm a minute off.
[00:00:08] Diego: diego, platform.
[00:00:10] Priya: priya, ops.
[00:00:12] Samir: great. lina and i will walk through latency/readiness questions — especially p95 and streaming. lina, you want to kick us off?
[00:00:20] Lina: yeah sure. so high level, neuroflux — want to confirm — you're targeting a p95 for interactive chat of about 400ms for short prompts, and for streaming transcripts p95 at 1.8s per message? is that still accurate?
[00:00:33] Aisha: that's right, for our clinical assistant flows short completions need to be snappy, sub 500ms ideally. for long streaming sessions (dictation -> note gen) we accept higher tail latency but we need consistency, 2 seconds is kinda our upper bound.
[00:00:44] Diego: just to be explicit, those numbers are user-facing p95 end-to-end including network and our gateway. our infra usually adds ~80-120ms. so backend target to Redwood should be like p95 <= 320ms for short.
[00:00:58] Samir: perfect, that helps. and what's the concurrency pattern? steady state vs bursts?
[00:01:05] Aisha: steady state is small — maybe 20 concurrent users generating short completions. bursts are the problem: we did an internal A/B test where an event caused 600 concurrent users hitting text-gen within a 30s window. that created tail pain.
[00:01:18] Priya: during that event our plateau for token/sec peaked around 14k tokens/min per model instance; but because requests are bursty we saw cold starts and queueing.
[00:01:29] Lina: okay — so two signals: concurrency (20 steady, 600 burst) and token velocity. for streaming you mentioned per-session token rates?
[00:01:36] Aisha: streaming note: average stream emits ~70 tokens/sec for 20s, but some sessions go 3-4 minutes at 40-60 tps.
[00:01:46] Samir: thanks. for approach — hosted vs dedicated vs private: hosted gives fastest path to bench but shared capacity means noisy neighbor risk at extreme bursts, we have burst pools and autoscale but dedicated gives you reserved pods and more predictable p95; private/VPC is mostly about compliance and data residency.
[00:02:03] Diego: so for the burst scenario we want predictable p95 for our high tier customers. could Redwood do guaranteed capacity to hit backend p95 320ms for short completions under 600 concurrent?
[00:02:13] Lina: yes with Dedicated and a sizing buffer you can get predictable p95. realistically we'd model concurrency and batching — for short prompts batching is minimal, so we plan GPU allocation to meet that concurrency. we'd also recommend warm pools to avoid cold start tails.
[00:02:27] Aisha: curious about streaming, how does kv cache/prefix caching help? our token re-use is moderate but we have many repeated system prompts.
[00:02:34] Lina: prefix/KV cache helps a lot for repeated prefixes — it drops compute per token significantly. in streaming it reduces the cost and the latency for first few tokens when kv hits. but cache invalidation rules matter — if you vary system prompt often, benefit reduces.
[00:02:47] Priya: on security, we need SOC2 plus KMS integration and audit logs, also SAML SSO for RBAC. any gotchas?
[00:02:55] Samir: standard — hosted supports SOC2/ISO material, KMS integration for Dedicated and Private, audit logs are available in Console. for private we can do customer-managed keys/HSM in some cases. we'll send the SOC2 cert and a short security pack.
[00:03:08] Ben: (joining) sorry folks, wifi, ben here. quick q — model variants and graceful degradation: what happens when the high perf variant is saturated? do you fall back to a smaller model automatically?
[00:03:18] Lina: good question. we support policy-based routing. you can specify latency SLOs and fallback chains: e.g., gpt-13k-highperf -> gpt-13k-quantized -> 7b-quantized. fallback happens with config to preserve semantics or to degrade tokens. you can also require explicit approval for fallback in case of quality sensitivity.
[00:03:35] Diego: do fallbacks count toward the same SLA/billing?
[00:03:37] Samir: fallback requests are billed at the variant used. SLA is about the front-door experience — we track p95 for the route; customers often define separate SLOs per variant.
[00:03:47] Aisha: can you give rough numbers for tokens/sec and latency for the 13k model quantized on a T4-ish host vs a dedicated A100 pool?
[00:03:57] Lina: rough ballpark: on a modern A100 serving optimized kernels you might see 600-900 tokens/sec for sampling workloads at mid-length context (2k). quantized on Ampere T4 or equivalent might be 120-220 tokens/sec depending on kernel and sequence length. these are engineering ballparks; we'd propose running a targeted benchmark against your prompts.
[00:04:16] Priya: that gap is big. for us tokens/sec in stream matters because we have real-time constraints for dictation flows. if fallback halves token throughput that's a UX issue.
[00:04:25] Lina: understood; that's why we recommend a hybrid: keep a small dedicated pool for high SLO paths, let hosted/dedicated handle lower tiers. also autoscale with burst reserve helps absorb spikes.
[00:04:35] Samir: any constraints on network egress or data residency we should know of?
[00:04:39] Diego: we need EU-only residency for some customers, and per-tenant log retention rules. private deployment preferred for those.
[00:04:46] Samir: noted. for benchmarking — would you prefer we run a hosted synthetic bench first or give you a test harness to run in your env?
[00:04:53] Aisha: start hosted to validate latency curves quickly, but we'll want to run the same harness against our infra for end-to-end numbers. so both.
[00:05:00] Samir: perfect. we'll share a benchmark plan and a small harness (k6 script + token logger).
[00:05:05] Lina: i want to call out tail-latency mitigation: keep KV warm, prefer continuous batching windows of ~20-50ms for throughput efficiency, and enable warm pools for the small dedicated nodes.
[00:05:16] Priya: how do you measure p95 — is it per-token or per-response? we need per-user-event p95.
[00:05:21] Lina: we measure per-response at the inference router. you can also instrument per-token timing, but user-level p95 should map to the response finish time. we'll share our tracing docs.
[00:05:28] Diego: about pricing — how do you charge for reserved capacity vs burst?
[00:05:32] Samir: reserved capacity is monthly commit (instance-hours + baseline throughput) and bursts are usage-based on top. we can model a cost example in the pricing sketch.
[00:05:38] Ben: any prior customers with similar 600-user burst profiles? curious real-world lessons.
[00:05:42] Lina: yes — a telehealth customer had similar peaks. they used a small dedicated pool sized for 95% of peaks and configured fallback policies for the rare super-peaks; that reduced cost by ~35% vs permanently reserving enough capacity, and kept p95 within target for the dedicated tier. we can share anonymized numbers.
[00:05:58] Aisha: ok let's talk pilot scope: we want to validate backend p95 320ms for short prompts at 600 concurrency, and steady streaming end-to-end p95 <= 2s for 90% of sessions. proposed timeline?
[00:06:10] Samir: timeline: week 0 — baseline hosted synthetic bench (2-3 days), week 1 — dedicated pilot sizing and run (3-5 days), week 2 — if needed private proof (longer). we can compress if you prioritize.
[00:06:21] Diego: resources — we'll need security docs before committing to dedicated. also a draft pilot config and an estimated cost.
[00:06:28] Samir: yes. action items: we'll send SOC2 + security pack, benchmark harness and sheet, pricing sketch, and a suggested dedicated config.
[00:06:36] Priya: we might also want a perf deep-dive with one of your infra engineers on the kernel/quantization differences.
[00:06:41] Lina: sure, happy to do a deep dive. we can pair with your SRE and run profiling.
[00:06:45] Aisha: one more nuance — our data retention rules: transcripts are PII-adjacent, we need to purge logs after 30 days for certain customers. how does Redwood expose log retention?
[00:06:55] Samir: Console has retention settings at route level for logs and telemetry; for Hosted we have defaults but can scope longer/shorter retention; for Dedicated/Private you control retention and we support purge APIs. we'll include details in the security pack.
[00:07:07] Ben: quick nit — is there support for function/tool calling in streaming? we have a downstream toolchain that accepts chunked structured JSON.
[00:07:13] Lina: yes, function/tool calling is supported in streaming; we also support structured output enforcement and schema validation on the return path. small caveat: structured enforcement can add a tiny bit of latency due to validation, but typically under 10-20ms.
[00:07:27] Diego: about observability — will we get token-level cost and latency breakdowns?
[00:07:31] Tom (CSM): yes the Console exposes token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, trace linking, and export hooks to your datadog/splunk.
[00:07:40] Aisha: ok fine. let's finalize next steps and owners.
[00:07:44] Samir: recap then: Redwood to deliver security pack (SOC2, KMS notes), benchmark harness + instructions, a pricing sketch and a suggested dedicated sizing, and schedule a technical deep dive.
[00:07:56] Diego: timeline — can you get that to us by friday 12/12?
[00:07:59] Samir: yes, we'll aim for 12/12.
[00:08:02] Lina: i'll also set up an initial hosted bench run and share the sheet.
[00:08:06] Priya: we'll stand up a small test account and run your harness; send creds and instructions.
[00:08:11] Samir: perfect. any other blockers or questions?
[00:08:14] Aisha: nothing else, thanks.
[00:08:17] Ben: thanks everyone.
[00:08:20] Samir: great, we'll follow up.

(Recording continues with brief Q&A and clarifications; Ben asked about quantization compatibility at 00:18:30, Lina noted some model-specific quirks and that we'd run model-conversion tests.)

End of transcript.
